newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks to improve Japan ties during Santer visit.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks to improve Japan ties during Santer visit.

text.p: The European Union, chipping away at a $26 billion trade deficit with Japan, will seek to build on better relations with Tokyo during a visit by European Commission President Jacques Santer which begins on Tuesday.

Santer is leading a high-level team to Tokyo for the fifth annual EU-Japan summit during which he will meet Emperor Akihito, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto as well as leading economists, academics and business chiefs.

The importance the European Commission attaches to the visit is shown by Santer's punishing schedule which will see him in Japan for four days before flying directly to Dublin for the EU summit on October 5.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton -- who represents the current presidency of the EU -- will accompany him, but return to prepare for the summit a day earlier.
The EU has slowly been whittling down its trade deficit with Japan, which soared to over $40 billion in the late 1980s.

Figures from Eurostat, the EU's statistical office, show last year that Japan exported around $63.4 billion worth of goods to the 15-nation EU, a rise of 4.5 percent. Japanese imports from the EU rose 12.5 percent to $37.4 billion.
EU relations with Tokyo have for years been marked by rows over access to Japanese markets, allegations of dumping and disputes over standards and certification.
Although officials said most of these problems had been resolved, they warned this week they would not let up on pressing Japan to give the EU access to lucrative insurance and financial markets.

Santer's visit is not just concerned with trade. The EU is also pressing Tokyo to take a greater role in international issues ranging from peace efforts in the Middle East and Bosnia to easing developing world debt, of which Japan owns a considerable portion.

The EU is also keen to to discuss KEDO, the organisation for energy development in the Korean peninuslar. The Commission is considering financial aid for North Korea's nuclear industry on condition it is used only for the nation's civilian energy needs.
The Japan-EU summit will also discuss reform of the United Nations including the possibility of a permanent seat on the Security Council for Japan.

The agenda, however, is dominated by trade issues and the Commission hopes to make further progress on aligning EU and Japanese views ahead of the World Trade Organisation summit in Singapore in December.
The EU wants to press Tokyo on its inclusion in a U.S.-Japan semiconductor alliance which is threatening to hold up progress on a trilateral International Technology Agreement.
This issue is also being taken up in the fringes of the so-called "Quad meeting", which groups Canada, the U.S., the EU and Japan, currently meeting in Seattle, Washington.
